CONGRANT.TITLE: UTRGV-UMN PARTNERSHIP to Strengthen the PREM Pathway
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) located in the southernmost region of Texas serves over 31,000 students, of whom 89% are Hispanic. UTRGV is 2nd in the nation in total Hispanic enrollment and 3rd in graduating Hispanics. The proposed Partnership for Research and Education in Materials (PREM) between UTRGV and the University of Minnesota (UMN) Materials Research Science and Engineering Center (MRSEC) will focus particularly on retention and degree attainment of underrepresented minority undergraduates, as well as on building the graduate school pipeline where Hispanic students are even more underrepresented. The PREM pathway goals are to achieve a 5-year graduation rate of at least 85% for PREM undergraduate students and a graduate school enrollment rate of at least 30% for PREM alumni. This PREM aims to provide intensive research opportunities to at least 100 undergraduate students during the course of the award. Students will develop expertise in the broad areas of energy and smart materials while acquiring a strong set of multi-disciplinary skills in fundamental research. The participating students will carry out research at both academic institutions and will be mentored by faculty from several disciplines. Mentoring of junior and mid-career faculty will also be fostered. This PREM program will allow UTRGV to significantly accelerate its emergence as a focal center for materials research and develop a long-lasting collaborative partnership with UMN. The research results under the UTRGV-UMN PREM partnership will be disseminated in peer-reviewed journals and conferences, and to the public at large via a dedicated web portal and frequent presentations at local K-12 schools.

The UTRGV-UMN PREM will engage in compelling scientific materials research through a synergistic approach towards development of next-generation nanofiber (NF) systems that could impact a large number of important practical applications, including in the biomedical fields, filtration, electronics and energy related sectors. The team proposes to develop a suite of strategies to prescribe, tailor, design and control the mesostructures of fine fibers. UTRGV’s world leadership in force-spinning leverages its platform in NF process-structure-characterization, while design and characterization of nanoscale structures match a distinguishing strength of the UMN MRSEC. The team will produce tunable hierarchical structures with powerful property combinations. The proposed research is organized around two interdisciplinary research groups (IRG); the first will explore processing routes to control both fiber geometry and internal structure, and the second will adapt internally structured NFs for specific applications. The world-class instrument facilities at UMN will enable and catalyze the research efforts and will provide unique opportunities for cross-fertilization of ideas, mentoring, and multidisciplinary training. The collaborative teams will hold research-focus group meetings via real-time video teleconferencing and hold an annual symposium hosted by each institution, rotating yearly. This will foster a high-level of research activity and a well-orchestrated student-centered organizational environment. Ultimately, this research partnership will increase understanding of hierarchically designed NFs and will pave the way for novel systems with potential to facilitate decentralized energy production in the world.

CONGRANT.TITLE: REU SITE: Interdisciplinary Research Experience for Undergraduates in Materials Science and Engineering at UTRGV
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This REU Site award to the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) will support the training of diverse undergraduate students in cutting edge research for 10 weeks during the summers of 2025-2027. A total of 30 students will be supported by the REU site in a three-year comprehensive engineering research activity. The students will be exposed to hands-on learning experience in the basics of materials science and engineering, involved in cutting-edge multidisciplinary research activities with aim to enrich their skills in the interrelationship between structure-processing-properties and performance of materials and nano/biomaterials. Exposure to these engineering research frontiers will arouse the students’ interest in pursuing higher education and considerably help increase both the number of students who choose engineering as their careers andthe education standards of UG students from minority and underrepresented groups across the USA. The REU site will also expand the knowledge and understanding of the technical projects by the students to develop and use diverse materials in real applications. The impact of this project will be already broadened by the direct participation of a HSI in engineering (UTRGV) as well as enhancing and maintaining an engineering-going (and a college-going) culture in a Hispanic- concentrated population. The REU site will also change the stereotypical gender and race assumptions in engineering and STEM study and career choice, especially for underrepresented Hispanic and women students. The proposed research activities will benefit society and national interest by advancing the existing knowledge in materials science and engineering and supporting diversity, research, and education at the national level.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Understanding the structure-processing-properties relationship of novel hyper organic/inorganic materials for catalytic applications
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Alumina (Al2O3) is widely used as catalyst support media in the Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) processes of crude oil due to its textural properties such as surface area and their acid/base characteristics. However, the chemical and hydrothermal stability of Al2O3 are still a critical point for catalytic applications due to many challenges, which may block the active sites of the catalyst resulting in catalyst instability. Strategies for minimizing these problems have involved the use of carbon, TiO2, silica and carbon nanotubes as alternative catalyst supports due to their high surface area, strong metal support interaction, and acid-base properties. This proposal  involves the use of Forcespinning (FS) of a high melting point polymer to fabricate polymer/ceramic composite fibers as a catalyst support in heterogeneous catalysis. The current proposal focuses on establishing a fundamental understanding of the relationships between processing, structure, composition, and performance of polymer fibers to improve the manufacturability of the material and to understand how the interaction between the polymer fibers and catalyst nanoparticles. Successful demonstration of the proposed work will lead to new understanding of the fundamental questions: Can polymer-supported catalysts extend the catalysis operational range beyond its current capabilities? and Can polymer-supported catalysts provide a significant advancement in understanding the behavior of catalyst support materials under operating conditions?  Our hypothesis is that unlike traditionally extruded oxide supported catalysts, polymer forcespun-supported catalysts should have lighter weights, higher activity, better packing densities resulting in longer life times for the catalysts.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of a Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) for Advanced Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
PROJECT SUMMARY

Overview:
The objective of the present MRI proposal is to acquire a state-of-the-art Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) that will support interdisciplinary research and education programs at UTRGV. The STEM combines the principles of transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed instrument (Talos™ F200i) is flexible and compact 200 kV Field Emission Gun (FEG) STEM, designed for precise and quantitative characterization of nanomaterials and biological cells. It combines an outstanding quality in high-resolution STEM imaging with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). In addition, the instrument is equipped with tomographic capabilities via software for alignment of a tomographic series of images, and 3D reconstruction of the data.

Intellectual Merit:
The acquisition of the Talos™ F200i STEM instrument will enable a significant enhancement of basic research toolset across a wide range of materials, medical education and research programs including Chemistry, Physics, Medicine and Mechanical, Electrical and Manufacturing Engineering at UTRGV. Specifically, the proposed equipment will support projects to advance the development and characterization of different nanoparticles as lubricant additives, composite nanofibers, high entropy alloys (HEA) prepared by Selective Laser Melting technology, regenerative medicine, polymers, and nanomaterials for use in , patterned magnetic arrays, temperature controlled drug delivery systems, bioimaging, nanostructured energetic devices, semiconductors, high temperature superconductors, and radiation induced functional materials. The acquisition of the STEM will broaden the research scope for all participants, making it possible to address new scientific challenges in new transformative research directions.

Broader Impacts:
This proposal brings together a diverse group of faculty members and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. In addition, most of the projects will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the instrument will strengthen existing courses and several more will be developed as a result of this funding. Additionally, it will significantly support research and education programs operated at the DoD I-DREAM4D Consortium, which was recently funded by DoD on a $4 million grant and NSF PREM funded projects. It can also be integrated in the K12 outreach and education efforts organized by the colleges and the consortium at national scale. Results from the research projects supported by this instrument will be disseminated in peer journal articles and national/international conferences to stimulate further understanding and progress of the various research areas of the investigators discussed in this proposal. More importantly, this proposal will:1) Promote a hands-on, entrepreneurial, educational experience, and training of graduate and undergraduate students in advanced materials, nanomaterial design, biomaterials and characterization; 2) Enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV; 3) Enhance the interdisciplinary research partnership between different departments at UTRGV to better compete for external funding; and 4) Increase the Hispanic Student retention rate at UTRGV

In summary, the Talos™ F200i instrument acquisition will strengthen the existing materials and medical research infrastructure at UTRGV and enhance the research and educational experiences of many students at UTRGV and South Texas region.

MRI: Acquisition of a single crystal/powder X-ray diffractometer
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The objective of this grant application is to acquire a cutting-edge single crystal/powder X-ray diffractometer SC-XRD/PXRD to support fundamental and interdisciplinary research projects and the education program in the South Texas region. The instrument will be installed at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and will support to a broad range of users and will be used as shared instrumentation. The goal of this acquisition is to enable the following: (i) Pursue new research avenues; (ii) Advance current research programs; and (iii) Enhance pedagogical techniques and enrich training in the undergraduate and graduate programs in STEM field.
The X-ray diffractometer system will buttress the development of advanced materials at UTRGV in an array of applications, including, but not limited to, electrocatalysis, lithium-ion batteries, molecular catalysis, and ferromagnetic materials. These diverse research thrusts would be substantially aided by state-of-the-art X-ray diffraction with overarching applications in sensors, energy storage, environmental sustainability, protein characterization, organic methodology, and disease diagnosis/treatment. The single crystal X-ray diffractometer allows for the unambiguous determination of the solid-state structure of molecular materials including accurate data on the 3D spatial arrangements of atoms, molecules, the interatomic distance between atoms, bond angles and neighboring atoms.
UTRGV is a Hispanic Serving Institution located in South Texas and has the largest Hispanic student population (~90%) in Texas. Individuals from Hispanic ethnicity are historically underrepresented in the STEM workforce and in higher education STEM-disciplines. Faculty members spanning several departments at UTRGV will directly use the requested system for their existing and new research projects as well as the training of highly qualified personnel. Graduate and undergraduate students are expected to take on a leadership role in the proposed interdisciplinary research projects. The acquisition of the X-ray diffractometer will enhance existing outreach efforts with local High school students and teachers during the UTRGV’s summer design camp administered by the research team of this MRI proposal. These integrated activities will unequivocally strengthen research, education, and student participation across programs in chemistry, biology, physics and engineering at UTRGV. In addition, the SC-XRD system will become a tool to bolster regional collaboration of universities and community colleges in South Texas. The personnel exposed to the SC-XRD prioritize fostering an environment of equity and inclusion for underrepresented minority students.

Intellectual Merit: The SC-XRD instrument acquisition will enable significant enhancement of basic
research toolset across a wide range of materials characterization including but not limited to molecular catalysts, nanomaterials, stimuli-responsive assemblies, supramolecular materials, biological materials, and gas sensors. Determination of molecular structure allows for furthering fundamental understanding of structure-function studies in the interdisciplinary research thrusts in this proposal. Characterization of molecular materials ranging in size from well-defined small molecules to more complex biological systems and solid-state materials is a prerequisite to advance the knowledge of broad research directions at UTRGV.

Broader Impacts: The acquisition of the X-ray diffractometer will advance research at UTRGV in the broadly defined areas of materials and biomaterials. The X-ray diffractometer will also enhance the research/educational experience of undergraduate and graduate students at UTRGV from a wide array of science and engineering disciplines. Both the SC-XRD and PXRD will be heavily featured in course curriculum currently offered in the Chemistry, Engineering, and Physics department at UTRGV. The SC-XRD functionality specifically, will foster a research hub in the south-Texas region and bolster collaborative work between researchers at UTRGV and other schools in south Texas including Texas A&M Corpus Christi, Texas A&M Kingsville, and Texas A&M International University. Collaborative efforts between these HSI’s in the south Texas region, will enhance the participation and training of under-represented students in STEM-based disciplines. Continued efforts in outreach to local high schools and community colleges will be enhanced and further recruitment and preparation of local underrepresented populations. The team will ensure that inclusion of women and underrepresented minority students are prioritized in research and educational activities.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
There is a general lack of reliable data for the determination of the speciation and concentrations of
arsenic and selenium in coal and fly-Ash. To address these limitations, we propose new experimental
methods to perform a series of studies on coal and fly-Ash to determine the speciation and concentrations
of arsenic and selenium. The work described in this proposal involves the acquisition of an in-house
EXAFS system; an easyXAFS system. The combination of data collected from the easyXAFS system and
an existing Thermo Scientific XPS system will be utilized to perform a series of studies on coal and fly-
Ash to determine the speciation and concentrations of arsenic and selenium. The speciation studies will
be utilized both in research and teaching. These studies will be utilized to train undergraduate students in
XANES and XPS data collection and data analysis as it applies to coal and fly-ash analyses. Instrument
will supplement the teaching curriculum in the chemistry and mechanical engineering departments at
UTRGV. The overall objective of the proposed work is to develop a set of methods/techniques, for the
utilization of in-house XAS and XPS to examine both the concentration and speciation of arsenic and
selenium in coal and fly-ash samples. The PI and Co-PI will integrate XAS as a standard teaching and
research tool at UTRGV in the chemical sciences and mechanical engineering. The acquisition of the
easyXAFS system will provide for the training of approximately 60-80 minority STEM students
(Hispanic students) per year, for the duration of the grant and for the lifetime of the instrument. This will
be achieved through hands-on teaching with the instrument in courses offered in both, the Department of
Chemistry and the Department of Mechanical Engineering at UTRGV. This training will better prepare
UTRGV students to perform research and move forward in their careers as students or as professionals.
The proposed work will provide a unique opportunity, to the students in the chemistry and mechanical
engineering departments at UTRGV to carry out innovative research in the area characterization and
determination of concentrations of arsenic and selenium in coal and fly-Ash. . This opportunity was only
available to these students at a national laboratory.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Composite Inorganic and Organic Materials for Catalytic and Energy Systems
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Project Summary: Recently, specifically engineered nanomaterials with controlled morphology continue to attract significant interest. Numerous scientific endeavors such as environmental remediation, dye sensitized solar cells (DSSCs), and battery technology benefit from the added development of synthetic strategies to design specific nano-architectures using composite materials. However, the relationships between synthesis, structure, and function are not well understood. This research hopes to uncover valuable information to further develop a better understanding of the links between synthesis, structure, and function in photoactive zinc oxide (ZnO) composite nanomaterials in photo-catalysis, molecular junctions in DSSCs, and as anode materials for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). To properly utilize ZnO’s photoactive properties for the aforementioned applications, we need to synthesize ZnO crystal structures composed of nanorods, nanowires, nanospheres, and nanosheets (consisting of hexagonal ZnO platelets). Composite materials consisting of these ZnO morphologies on graphene, graphene oxide, and reduced graphene oxide supports have the potential to photocatalytically degrade environmental contaminants such as atrazine, simazine, hexachlorophenol, and BPA. Additionally, we will examine the use of conductive organic thin films patterned with gold nanoparticles at the interface to serve as seed sites for the growth of ZnO nanowires for the preparation of molecular junctions in DSSCs.Finally, the synthesized ZnO/graphene, ZnO/graphene oxide, and ZnO/reduced graphene oxide composites are immobilized in polymer fibers through centrifugal spinning and converted into carbonized mats for application in structured zinc oxide/carbon composite anode materials for battery production.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Synthesis, processing and characterization of novel hyper organic/inorganic materials for catalytic applications
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Alumina (Al2O3) is widely used as catalyst support media in the Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) processes of crude oil due to its textural properties such as surface area and their acid/base characteristics. However, the chemical and hydrothermal stability of Al2O3 are still a critical point for catalytic applications due to many challenges, which may block the active sites of the catalyst resulting in catalyst instability. Strategies for minimizing these problems have involved the use of carbon, TiO2, silica and carbon nanotubes as alternative catalyst supports due to their high surface area, strong metal support interaction, and acid-base properties. This proposal involves the use of Forcespinning (FS) of a high melting point polymer to fabricate polymer/ceramic composite fibers as a catalyst support in heterogeneous catalysis. Unlike traditionally extruded supported catalysts, the polymer forcespun-supported catalysts should have lighter weights, better packing resulting in longer life times for the catalysts. The better packing will result from the packing of polymer nonwoven mats into the catalytic beds instead of extruded cylindrical based pellets.
The current proposal focuses on establishing a fundamental understanding of the relationships between processing, structure, composition, and performance of polymer fibers to improve the manufacturability of the material and to understand how the interaction between the polymer fibers and catalyst nanoparticles. Successful demonstration of the proposed work will lead to new fabrication methods for polymer-supported catalyst that extend the catalysis operational range beyond its current capabilities and will provide a significant advancement in understanding the behavior of catalyst support materials under operating conditions.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This project aims to develop Ionic Liquid based electrolytes for use in Lithium-ion batteries. As we move away from energy produced from fossil fuels to those produced from renewable sources, such as solar energy and wind energy, energy storage is becoming an important problem that needs to be addressed in order for these sources to be more widely used. Batteries used for energy storage consist of a positive electrode, a negative electrode, and an electrolyte solution which allows the movement of positively and negatively charged ions (cations and anions) between the electrodes. Currently, Lithium-ion batteries are the most widely used batteries. One major limitation in further developing these batteries, is the current use of volatile, flammable and toxic compounds in the electrolyte medium. By developing new Ionic Liquids, we aim to gain a better understanding of the properties of Ionic Liquids, and develop better and safer batteries. The results of the study will be used for external grant applications and will be published in peer-reviewed journals and presented in national and international conferences.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: In the present work, the effect of temperature and additives on the ionic conductivity of mixed organic/ionic liquid electrolytes (MOILEs) was investigated by conducting galvanostatic charge/discharge and ionic conductivity experiments. The mixed electrolyte is based on the ionic liquid (IL) (EMI/TFSI/LiTFSI) and organic solvents EC/DMC (1:1 v/v). The effect of electrolyte type on the electrochemical performance of a LiCoO2 cathode and a SnO2/C composite anode in lithium anode (or cathode) half-cells was also investigated. The results demonstrated that the addition of 5 wt.% succinonitrile (SN) resulted in enhanced ionic conductivity of a 60% EMI-TFSI 40% EC/DMC MOILE from similar to 14 mS.cm(-1) to similar to 26 mS.cm(-1) at room temperature. Additionally, at a temperature of 100 degrees C, an increase in ionic conductivity from similar to 38 to similar to 69 mS.cm(-1) was observed for the MOILE with 5 wt% SN. The improvement in the ionic conductivity is attributed to the high polarity of SN and its ability to dissolve various types of salts such as LiTFSI. The galvanostatic charge/discharge results showed that the LiCoO2 cathode with the MOILE (without SN) exhibited a 39% specific capacity loss at the 50th cycle while the LiCoO2 cathode in the MOILE with 5 wt.% SN showed a decrease in specific capacity of only 14%. The addition of 5 wt.% SN to the MOILE with a SnO2/C composite-fiber anode resulted in improved cycling performance and rate capability of the SnO2/C composite-membrane anode in lithium anode half-cells. Based on the results reported in this work, a new avenue and promising outcome for the future use of MOILEs with SN in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) can be opened.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: We report results on the electrochemical performance of flexible and binder-free alpha-Fe2O3/TiO2/carbon composite fiber anodes for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). The composite fibers were produced via centrifugal spinning and subsequent thermal processing. The fibers were prepared from a precursor solution containing PVP/iron (III) acetylacetonate/titanium (IV) butoxide/ethanol/acetic acid followed by oxidation at 200 degrees C in air and then carbonization at 550 degrees C under flowing argon. The morphology and structure of the composite fibers were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). These ternary composite fiber anodes showed an improved electrochemical performance compared to the pristine TiO2/C and alpha-Fe2O3/C composite fiber electrodes. The alpha-Fe2O3/TiO2/C composite fibers also showed a superior cycling performance with a specific capacity of 340 mAh g(-1) after 100 cycles at a current density of 100 mA g(-1), compared to 61 mAh g(-1) and 121 mAh g(-1) for TiO2/C and alpha-Fe2O3/C composite electrodes, respectively. The improved electrochemical performance and the simple processing of these metal oxide/carbon composite fibers make them promising candidates for the next generation and cost-effective flexible binder-free anodes for LIBs.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: © 2016 Elsevier B.V. Nanocrystalline complex oxide scintillators have emerged for use in X-ray and gamma-ray detection in recent years. The quantum yield of the red emission was found to depend on the Eu 3+ doping concentration and excitation wavelength. Moreover, these La 2 Zr 2 O 7 :x%Eu 3+ NPs demonstrated an atypical Eu 3+ related scintillating response with a red emission under high-energy X-ray excitation with the scintillation intensity also depending on the Eu 3+ doping concentration. Finally, the irradiation damage behavior induced by the excitation source was representatively examined for the La 2 Zr 2 O 7 :5%Eu 3+ NPs. It is expected that the current study will pave the way for future research of nanoscintillators.

PRESENT.ABSTRACT: With the invention of the electric cars and the exponential growth in portable electronics over the last decade, energy storage systems that can supply and store more power are of utmost importance. Li-ion batteries (LIBs) entered the market less than a decade ago to keep up with market demands and have since become the most efficient way to store energy due to their reversible nature. Graphite is currently the most widely used material in (LIB) anodes due to its long cycle life and low manufacturing cost, its main drawback being its low theoretical capacity of 372 mAg-1. Metal oxides have been of interest as electrode materials for (LIBs) due to their inherently high theoretical capacities and low cost. However, the main drawback of metal oxide-based anodes includes high volume expansion, particle agglomeration, and dendrite formation. Developments in composites and novel micro/nano-structures that withstand large temperature ranges and maintain structural stability have attracted interest for their use as electrode materials in LIBs. Here, we explore the performance of Iron Oxide (Fe2O3), Tin Oxide (SnO2), Zinc Oxide (ZnO), and Cobalt Oxide (Co3O4), coated on carbon fibers as hosts for lithium ion insertion/de-insertion during charge/discharge process. The synthesis and design of Fe2O3/Carbon and SnO2/C composite fibers were reiliazed by the centrifugal spinning of metal-oxides precursors in polyacrylonitrile (PAN)/ dimethylformamide (DMF) solutions and followed by calcination at 600 °C in an inert gas. The characterization of Fe2O3/C, ZnO/C, Co3O4/C and SnO2/C composite fibers was conducted using X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive X-ray analysis (EDAX). The pre-coated carbon fibers with metal-oxide nanoparticle precursors showed improved electrochemical performance compared to the pristine composite carbon-fibers anodes.
